card.title: Five Deaths and Delayed Compensation on Zanzibar's Drainage Works
card.place: Mwanakwerekwe and Stone Town, Unguja, Zanzibar, Tanzania

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Zanzibar Urban Services Project (P111155), Credit IDA-48610 of US$38 million approved 24 February 2011 and Credit IDA-58430 of US$55 million as additional financing in June 2016, SDR 63.9 million in all; US$87.57 million disbursed; closed 31 May 2021, five years after its first closing date. The credit paid the compensation costs under the project's resettlement plans because the government could not, and the Bank approved a further US$550,000 of project money to pay the Kibele landfill compensation. The completion report rates the outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation Substantial (23 November 2021); the Evaluation Group's review rates the outcome Satisfactory and Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, where the completion report rates Bank performance Satisfactory. The completion report's table of supervision reports shows the project's development objective and implementation progress both rated Moderately Unsatisfactory in the report archived on 9 July 2013, back to Moderately Satisfactory by March 2014 and Satisfactory at closing; the report gives no separate rating for safeguards compliance.

companies.name: Project Management Team, Ministry of Finance and Planning, Revolutionary Government of Zanzibar
companies.role: Ran the works and the resettlement plans; took statements after each fatal accident and agreed corrective measures with the lender
companies.desc: A unit inside Zanzibar's finance ministry set up to run this project; the completion report says it had no authority over the other ministries and agencies involved.

companies.name: Zanzibar Municipal Council
companies.role: Operated the waste dump site, demolished and compensated one house to open a route for collection vehicles, and began open dumping of waste in Ng'ambo settlements after the dump site closed
companies.desc: The municipal authority for Zanzibar Town, responsible for waste collection in the urban area.

card.community: Five people died in three accidents on the drainage works between 2015 and 2020. The completion report says the project "encountered weaknesses on the implementation of health and safety issues which led to three severe accidents and five fatalities". A trespasser who broke into a drainage work site through a gap in the fence fell and drowned on 3 April 2016. Two workers died when the soil collapsed at a deep cut on 8 November 2019. Two passengers on a motorcycle died when it crashed into a dump truck working near the Mwanakwerekwe pond on 22 March 2020. After each accident the project team took statements from contractors, workers, consultants and other witnesses, reported to the lender, and agreed corrective measures; the report says site safety and health management improved after those measures. On land and money, the drainage designs were revised during the project and the number of people affected and the cost came out far above the plan; the government could not pay and no land was available for land-for-land swaps, so the credit paid instead. The report says 605 people were compensated for the drainage and solid waste works, "albeit with some delays". A further 167 people in the buffer zone of the Kibele landfill faced delays and incomplete payment because the government budget ran short; after the lender released another US$550,000, all but three had been paid by 1 April 2021. A footnote records that those three could not be reached through radio, newspapers, village leaders "and so on", and that after the loan account closed at the end of September 2021 the government is obliged to pay them if they come forward to claim. The resettlement plan of December 2018 for drainage system C counted 194 affected households and 162 structures, 30 of them to be taken completely: 141 residential structures, of which 30 would be taken entirely and 111 would lose a wall, a verandah, a foundation, a room, a toilet, an outside kitchen or a septic tank; 12 businesses to be closed and moved, among them six at Sogea and shops at Shaurimoyo, Jitimai and Magogoni; and shelters used by widows, disabled people and people with long illnesses who the plan says would need help to move. The November 2017 plan for the Kibele landfill counted 60 individual landholders, of whom 13 living in occupied dwellings, with 57 household members, were to be moved out of the project area. The municipal council demolished one house, with compensation, to open a route for collection vehicles into a dense settlement where people had been throwing their rubbish into the drain. The Evaluation Group also records that the existing dump site, which the project had assumed would last five years, was closed during the project by community opposition unconnected to the project, after which the council "began open dumping of waste in Ng'ambo settlements causing an environmental and public health crisis".
card.killed_note: The five deaths are counted because the completion report gives a cause for each that ties it to the works: a gap in the fence at a drainage site, a soil collapse at a deep cut, and a dump truck working near the Mwanakwerekwe pond. The report attributes the three accidents to weaknesses in carrying out health and safety measures. The Evaluation Group's review repeats all three accounts.
card.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 14 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people. The World Bank's completion report counts 605 people compensated for the drainage and waste works and 167 more in the Kibele landfill buffer zone. It does not count the people moved. The counts of 194 households, 162 structures and 13 dwellings come from the project's resettlement plans and are what was planned.
card.outcome: The project closed on 31 May 2021 with an outcome rating of Satisfactory. Three people in the Kibele landfill buffer zone had still not been paid when the loan account closed at the end of September 2021, and the government was notified of its obligation to pay them in future. The completion report says overall safeguards management, occupational health and site safety improved after the accidents.
card.confidence_note: The five deaths, the compensation delays and the three people never reached are recorded in the World Bank's own completion report and repeated in its Evaluation Group's review of that report. No independent report of the deaths was found; searches of Tanzanian and Zanzibari press in English and Swahili returned nothing on them. The household and structure counts come from the borrower's own resettlement plans and are what was planned, not what was carried out.

card.whole: The credit built 20,718 metres of storm water drains outside Stone Town against a target of 21,800, a landfill of 425,000 cubic metres and 340 metres of sea wall and promenade at Mizingani, and US$87.57 million was spent. By the Bank's own count households suffering flooding in the municipal area fell from 3,645 to 64, people with rubbish collection rose from 75,600 to 187,200, and 412,914 people were counted as direct beneficiaries. One planned piece of work was dropped at the second restructuring: upgrading in the Ng'ambo area, which was to give 3,246 households access to infrastructure and services. No independent check of these figures was found.
card.conditions: The project agreement of August 2016, which covers both the original Credit 4861-TZ and the additional Credit 5843-TZ, required the Revolutionary Government of Zanzibar as implementing entity to carry out the project in accordance with the safeguard documents, and barred any activity needing a resettlement action plan from being implemented until the plan had been prepared, disclosed and approved by the Association, until all measures the plan required beforehand had been taken "including, without limitation to the above, providing funds for resettlement compensation when and if required under a RAP", and until the Association had confirmed the activity could start (World Bank, Project Agreement for Credit 5843-TZ and Credit 4861-TZ, Schedule, Section I.C.2(b)). The matching financing agreement defines the compensation owed as covering land taken, compulsory relocation or loss of shelter, lost assets, lost income or means of livelihood, and restricted access to parks and protected areas, and no safeguard document could be amended or waived without the Association's prior written approval. These are the terms in force from August 2016: the original financing agreement for Credit 4861-TZ, which that agreement dates 6 April 2011, has not been published, and the August 2016 terms therefore came in after the first of the five deaths, the drowning of 3 April 2016, and before the two deaths of 8 November 2019 and the two of 22 March 2020.

card.title: Kariakoo Terminal Site Cleared for the Dar es Salaam Bus Rapid Transit
card.place: The Kariakoo bus terminal site and the Ubungo bus depot site, Dar es Salaam, Tanzania

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-44550 of SDR 115.4 million (US$190 million equivalent) and Credit IDA-51850 of SDR 64.9 million (US$100 million equivalent) for the Second Central Transport Corridor Project (P103633), the second credit being the additional financing approved 15 January 2013 and carried under its own number P124114. Approved 27 May 2008, effective 28 November 2008, mid-term review 30 July 2010, closing extended from 31 December 2011 to 31 December 2016. The project financed Phase 1 of the Dar es Salaam bus rapid transit system and work at Tanzanian airports. The Government of Tanzania was to finance resettlement, entered in the completion report's cost and financing tables at US$10.7 million both at appraisal and at the additional financing, of which US$10.3 million, 96.2 per cent, was spent; a footnote elsewhere in the same report gives the Government's resettlement contribution as US$10.0 million. Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01) and Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12) were triggered. The completion report of 7 November 2017 rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, risk to development outcome Substantial, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, with quality at entry Moderately Unsatisfactory and quality of supervision Moderately Satisfactory, and borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR0021021 recorded the same ratings with no disagreement and rated the quality of the completion report Substantial. The implementing agencies were the Dar Rapid Transit Agency and the Tanzania National Roads Agency.

companies.name: Tanzania National Roads Agency
companies.role: The executive agency responsible for Tanzania's trunk and regional roads, which held fiduciary oversight of the project and ran the works contracts. The completion report says the census of project-affected people and property valuation were done before contractors were engaged, and that the agency's own account credits the Bank's local office with a leadership role among donors.
companies.desc: A Tanzanian government executive agency whose roles the national audit office cites from Rule 3(3) of the Executive Agencies (The Tanzania National Roads Agency) (Amendment) Order No. 350 of 2009, and whose performance on road maintenance the Ministry of Works and Transport oversees. The Roads Act, 2007 requires it, as a roads authority, to prepare and implement short and long-term road maintenance programmes. The audit, citing the Roads Fund Board's annual report of June 2019, records it as maintaining a national network of 36,258 km — 12,176 km of trunk roads and 24,082 km of regional roads, of which 1,756 km were paved.

companies.name: Dar Rapid Transit Agency
companies.role: The government agency set up to deliver and oversee the bus rapid transit system in Dar es Salaam, named in the completion report as an implementing agency alongside the roads agency.

card.community: The project built the first phase of the Dar es Salaam bus rapid transit system, which required a terminal at Kariakoo and a bus depot at Ubungo. The completion report states that the total number of project-affected people was 877 at the start and later rose to 1,236, and that the actual resettlement plan budget was TZS 23.5 billion, about US$11 million. Serious problems emerged with compensation. In January 2011, on an implementation support mission, the Bank team learned that insufficient funds had been allocated to meet the commitments under the resettlement plan. The inadequate funding and legal disputes, including a court injunction, led to contractual disputes and the termination of two works contracts, for the Kariakoo terminal and the Ubungo depot, because the sites were not available to the contractors. Two feeder transfer stations were not acquired at all and the operational design had to be changed. The plan was updated in March 2012 and the Ministry of Finance increased the money available, and the Government introduced a communications outreach strategy and set up a grievance redress mechanism. The people affected at the Kariakoo terminal site had filed a court case in 2008 and obtained an injunction blocking the Government from accessing the site. The completion report states that the site, with 106 families in semidetached buildings, was nonetheless cleared by the Government in March 2012 after the High Court dismissed their application for an injunction on technical grounds. They filed a separate civil suit and sought a further injunction, and in December 2013 the High Court ruled formally releasing the site to the Government for public use as the terminal, while the main suit was still pending judgment. The report records that the main case was still pending judgment in 2017, eight years after it was filed. It also states that the compensation funds were deposited in an escrow account and that most of the affected people had already claimed their compensation, and that a Tanzanian practising lawyer attended the court hearings as an observer for the Bank. The report says insufficient funding was set aside for the costs of compensation and relocation of project-affected people. Phase 1 of the system was expected to displace 1,800 existing minibuses, known as daladala, whose owners were to be compensated through preferential access to bus rapid transit routes and through payment for scrapped vehicles; the report says only a fraction of the daladala had been displaced as of end-2016. After initial construction, flash flooding occurred at Jangwani along the Msimbazi river basin, which analysis attributed to rapid siltation of the basin from uncontrolled encroachment, solid waste and human activity upstream; flood prevention measures were taken, and a more permanent solution involving the relocation of petty traders was left to later phases.
card.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 2,862 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's completion report counts 106 families in semidetached buildings at the Kariakoo terminal site, cleared by the Government in March 2012. The same report gives 877 project-affected people at the start, rising to 1,236, which is a count of people affected and not of people moved.
card.outcome: The credits closed on 31 December 2016, five years after the original date. The completion report of 7 November 2017 rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review agreed on both. The main court case brought by the people cleared from the Kariakoo site in 2008 was still awaiting judgment when the report was written in 2017; their compensation had been placed in escrow and the report says most of the affected people had claimed it. The report says that for later phases of the system the compensation resources are to be in place before works begin, and draws the lesson that adequate preparation of resettlement is a critical requirement.
card.confidence_note: The 106 families, the court history, the funding shortfall and the affected-person counts all come from the Bank's own completion report on its own project; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report adds no resettlement detail of its own. No independent press report or court judgment on the Kariakoo clearance was found. The report names no affected family, does not say how many people the 106 families contained, does not say where they went, and does not say how many of them had been paid when the site was cleared. It states that the compensation funds were placed in escrow and that most affected people had claimed their compensation. The completion report's cover page is dated 7 November 2017 while the Bank's document database and the file name give 7 December 2017.

sources.title: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Second Central Transport Corridor Project (P103633), ICR00004196
Independent Evaluation Group, ICR Review, TZ-Second Central Transport Corridor (P103633), ICRR0021021
World Bank, Project Appraisal Document, Second Central Transport Corridor Project (P103633), Report 43399
Performance Audit Report on Maintenance of Roads
sources.publisher: Controller and Auditor General, United Republic of Tanzania

card.whole: The bus rapid transit works were finished by December 2015, 100 per cent complete by value, and interim operations began on 10 May 2016. Rush-hour travel time between Ubungo and the central business district fell from 62 to 28 minutes against a target of 25. The service ran well below plan: 140 buses were operating at closing against a revised target of 248 and an original 305, and public transport passengers through Jangwani came to 162,000 a day against a target of 360,000 and a baseline of 250,000, with an estimated 200,000 more carried by daladalas on the parallel route; users along the corridor rated the service Moderately Satisfactory against a Satisfactory target, being least satisfied with waiting times. The airport side of the project finished the Zanzibar runway rehabilitation in August 2010, ahead of schedule, and the airport met the target of a satisfactory rating from airlines and passengers in a survey. The cost of the bus rapid transit roadworks rose 70 per cent from US$110 million to US$177 million between appraisal and the 2012 restructuring, and the completion report's ex-post economic rate of return, worked out at the actual average ridership of 125,809 a day, is 1.8 per cent, against 14.5 per cent at appraisal and 12.4 per cent at restructuring; the same model gives 8.4 per cent at 250,000 riders a day and 18 per cent at the 524,000 planned. All of these figures come from the lender's own completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it; no independent check was found.
card.conditions: The project triggered Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01) and Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12). The safeguard instruments were an environmental and social impact assessment and a Resettlement Action Plan built from a census, a property survey and a socio-economic survey of residents and businesses, with environmental and social management plans for all components. The Government of Tanzania was to finance resettlement costs from its own funds, entered in the completion report's cost table as US$10.7 million and in a footnote to another table as US$10.0 million. The completion report records that because the census and property valuation were carried out before the contractors were engaged, and because the money set aside to compensate affected people was insufficient, implementing the resettlement plan was difficult; it was updated in March 2012 and the Ministry of Finance increased the funds, and a grievance redress mechanism and a communications outreach strategy were set up at that point rather than at the start (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 7 November 2017).

phrases_already_tried: The Kariakoo bus terminal site and the Ubungo bus depot site

card.title: Himachal Pradesh State Roads Project: landslides, debris, and land occupied beyond what was acquired
card.place: Himachal Pradesh core road network, India

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loans IBRD-48600 (US$220 million approved 5 June 2007, US$219,998,008 disbursed) and IBRD-81990, an additional loan of US$61.7 million cut to US$46.7 million, all disbursed, for the Himachal Pradesh State Roads Project (P096019). Effective 5 October 2007; closing moved from 30 June 2013 to 30 June 2017. The state paid US$98.51 million of the US$365.21 million total (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 20 December 2017).

card.community: The Bank's completion report says land acquisition and resettlement 'often was slow', and gives the reasons as poor coordination between the implementing corporation and the Land Acquisition Officer, inaccurate information about land holdings in the resettlement action plans, mismatches between road design drawings and revenue maps, changes of alignment, and delays in negotiations and payments. In a footnote the report records that the Bank rated social safeguards performance Moderately Unsatisfactory at two consecutive supervision missions in 2008 and 2009, because the post of social development officer in the implementing corporation was vacant, no NGO was in place to deliver resettlement and rehabilitation assistance, and the corporation failed to act on allegations that contractors had occupied private land in excess of what had been acquired. The report says those problems were eventually remedied. Of the total compensation due, 96.2 per cent had been paid when the loan closed on 30 June 2017. The report says the amounts left unpaid on packages 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 were for reasons outside the corporation's control: owners had died with heirs not yet on record, there were court cases or stays, and co-owners were in dispute. Of the total resettlement and rehabilitation assistance due, 93.5 per cent had been paid; the report gives the reasons for the rest as owners not coming to collect despite notices, court cases, and people who could not be traced. The report gives no number of project-affected people anywhere. About 12 km of road were cut from several packages because of land acquisition problems. A survey of affected people on the ten upgrading packages in October, November and December 2016 found women recipients reporting nearly 100 per cent positive answers on better access to work, public services, safety and markets.
card.suppression: No arrests, forced evictions or police action are recorded in the Bank's completion report or the Independent Evaluation Group review.
card.killed_note: No deaths are recorded in the Bank's completion report, which does record workplace safety among the problems on four contracts.
card.displaced_note: No count of displaced people appears in the World Bank completion report; the results framework sets a land acquisition target of 132 hectares and 154 hectares of forest land diverted. ICIJ's 'Evicted and Abandoned' table gives 16,896, listed as an estimate of people displaced and taken from World Bank project documents as of 31 December 2014. There is no Bank figure here to set against ICIJ's.
card.outcome: The Bank rated the project's outcome Moderately Satisfactory. 355 km of the state core road network were upgraded from single to two lanes, against a target of 447 km. Environmental performance was rated Moderately Unsatisfactory for several months from late 2014 over what the Independent Evaluation Group calls 'serious problems' on contracts 5-I, 5-II, 6-I and 6-II: poor debris management, protection of forest lands, dust pollution, road safety and workplace safety. The completion report records that in September 2011 poor planning and sequencing of works on contract 9 caused several large landslides that blocked access for vehicles and people, and that an unprecedented landslide later delayed the same contract, forcing the contractor to remove debris and repair damaged pavement. About 80 debris disposal sites were later rehabilitated using bioengineering, and 432,692 trees were planted with a 69.75 per cent survival rate.
card.confidence_note: Everything here comes from the Bank's own completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it. The lender is reporting on its own project. No named community, court record, press report or NGO field research on this project was found. The completion report gives no count of affected people, read in full from the 56-page report, so the scale of the land taking cannot be checked against ICIJ's estimate. The documented harm here is environmental and procedural: the Bank's own Moderately Unsatisfactory environmental rating over debris management and forest protection, landslides caused by poor sequencing of works, and the 2008-2009 finding that the implementing corporation did not act on allegations that contractors had taken more private land than was acquired. The unpaid residuals of 3.8 per cent of compensation and 6.5 per cent of resettlement assistance are small shares of the total and the Bank attributes them to deaths, court cases and untraceable owners rather than to the project; they are not presented here as a compensation failure.

sources.title: India - Himachal Pradesh State Roads Project: Implementation Completion and Results Report
ICR Review: India - IN: HP State Roads Project (P096019)
Evicted and Abandoned: Himachal Pradesh State Roads Project (P096019)

card.whole: Alongside the upgraded roads, the Bank's completion report counts periodic maintenance awarded on 1,831 km against a target of about 2,000 km, 25 accident blackspots treated against a target of 20, and a road accident database running in every district of the state by July 2015. It says average speeds on the upgraded roads rose from 29 to 40 km/h, an increase of 38 per cent against a 25 per cent target, that the share of the state's core network in poor condition fell from 40 per cent to 10.4 per cent, and that deaths in traffic accidents per 1,000 vehicles fell from 0.28 in 2014 to 0.21 in 2017. No outcome indicator for transport costs was set when the project was appraised, so a proxy was used at closing: average vehicle operating cost of 9.78 rupees per kilometre against a pre-project 14.39, a 32 per cent reduction. The state did not create the road fund the project had planned, and the share of permanent gang labour in maintenance spending fell only from 75 to 62 per cent against a 50 per cent target. All these figures are the Bank's. The report's economic rate of return was 26 per cent at completion, covering 88 per cent of project cost, against 27 per cent at appraisal covering 78 per cent. The Independent Evaluation Group, the Bank's internal evaluators, agreed with the Moderately Satisfactory outcome rating and with the Moderately Satisfactory rating of Bank performance, but rated the project's efficiency Modest in spite of that return because of the cost and time overruns, and cut the rating of the project's monitoring from Substantial to Modest. No independent check was found.
card.conditions: The project was environmental category A and triggered five safeguard policies: environmental assessment, natural habitats, physical cultural resources, involuntary resettlement and forests. Resettlement action plans were prepared for each road package and an NGO was engaged to help carry them out. The additional loan's project agreement added a covenant on the implementing corporation.
card.ecosystem: 154 hectares of forest land were diverted for the roads. Environmental performance was rated Moderately Unsatisfactory for months over poor debris management and failure to protect forest lands on four contracts, and poor sequencing of works caused landslides on one contract in September 2011. Himachal Pradesh is a steep Himalayan state where the construction season is about six months a year.

card.title: Compensation Nine Months Late in Tanzania's Strategic Cities
card.place: Mbeya, Arusha, Ilemela, Mwanza, Kigoma-Ujiji, Dodoma, Tanga and Mtwara, Tanzania

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits IDA-47270 of US$163 million, IDA-54600 of US$50 million and IDA-59470 of US$130 million for the Tanzania Strategic Cities Project (P111153), SDR 236.2 million in all, about US$343 million. Approved 27 May 2010, effective 8 September 2010, mid-term review 8 May 2017. Original closing was 31 December 2015; actual closing was 26 November 2020, with a restructuring on 4 May 2020 extending the closing date. US$340,372,832 was disbursed of US$342,997,608 revised. Denmark was listed at approval as providing US$12.5 million and the completion report's financing table records nil for it at completion. There was no borrower contribution. The implementing agency was the Prime Minister's Office - Regional Administration and Local Government, renamed the President's Office - Regional Administration and Local Government during the project, working through the local government authorities of the participating cities. The completion report of 13 May 2021 rated outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation quality Substantial; the Independent Evaluation Group's review also rated outcome Satisfactory (Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00005449, 13 May 2021; IEG ICR Review, Bank document date 22 October 2021).

companies.name: President's Office - Regional Administration and Local Government (PO-RALG)
companies.role: The arm of the Tanzanian presidency that supervises regional administrations and local government authorities, and the project's implementing agency. It reviewed and monitored the resettlement action plans the local authorities prepared, wrote the project's grievance redress manual and trained the grievance handling committees (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 13 May 2021).
companies.desc: The Tanzanian government office that runs regional administration and local government: its own site says it oversees the 26 regions of Tanzania, ensures efficient coordination between the central government and local authorities, empowers local councils, districts, municipalities and cities, and oversees and implements projects in health, education and infrastructure, which it describes as expanding roads, water supply and public facilities.

card.community: The project rebuilt roads, drains, bus stands, markets and landfills in eight Tanzanian local government areas. Each subproject had its own resettlement action plan, and the plans of March 2010 count what was to be taken. In Mbeya, the census for the city roads subproject found that the assets mostly affected were 35 buildings including fences and six areas with crops, and that 41 people would be affected; the plan's entitlement table says people without formal legal rights to the land are to be paid full replacement cost for their assets but nothing for land, because they are encroachers along the road reserve. In Arusha, 279 households were to be affected by the proposed upgrading works, 136 of them owning structures and land except for 42 households at the Murriet dumpsite who were entitled to compensation for structures only, 248 owning crops at four locations, 20 households owning land only, and 13 administrators acting for 23 deceased and a shrine; at Urundini two households were to lose their houses and a third his incomplete house, and at the Murriet dumpsite four households owned eight commercial structures and two of the residential houses to be removed were traditional thatched msonge houses. The Arusha plan records that corridors of 16 or 25 metres were contemplated, that a 16-metre corridor was proposed where the houses affected were concentrated, that even at 16 metres a number of houses would have to be partially demolished, and that owners of partly affected houses were concerned about their fate and felt they would be treated in future as encroachers in the road reserve if they were not resettled, a matter the plan says ought to be addressed at the second round of consultations. The Dodoma plan says about 29 households at Kikuyu and 21 at Chidaya village would have houses or other property affected, which at the plan's own average of 4.3 people a household it turns into about 100 people affected by the upgrading of the Kisasa community roads, and that among the affected structures are dwelling houses and several graveyards. It says 3 buildings and 20 farmlands were to be compensated at the Chidaya landfill site. It records that there were no resettlement issues on the Kisasa community roads because the people living along them had been required to leave the right of way since 2002, years before this project began, but that to conform to the Bank's guidelines those who had stayed on would qualify for a token relief; all of them had been given plots for relocation close to their original plots, and the city development authority had agreed to pay each household Tshs 400,000, made up of Tshs 300,000 for accommodation and Tshs 100,000 for transport. The completion report gives the outcome. It says the subprojects complied with the resettlement action plans but faced challenges because the local government authorities fell short in paying compensation and because designs changed, and that 'RAP implementation was often delayed sometimes to over nine months when LGAs lacked funds for compensation of PAPs thus delaying construction activities and raising complaints by PAPs.' It says another problem arose when subproject designs changed, especially on drainage, which changed who was affected, and that remedial actions were identified in the resettlement plan completion reports. Separately it records that insufficient counterpart funding from the local authorities was an ongoing issue through the life of the project, and that acquiring land for the sanitary landfill buffer zones in Mwanza, Kigoma-Ujiji and Mbeya and the road corridor wayleaves for Ilemela and Arusha all had periods when implementation was delayed for want of counterpart funds, despite repeated engagement between the Bank, the local authorities, the President's Office and the Treasury. It adds that delay in utility removal and compensation was revealed to be a source of grievances. Grievance handling committees were set up in all subproject areas and kept logbooks, but the report says the project included no grievance procedure at contractor level, which could have helped resolve and monitor complaints by workers, and that the grievance mechanism as a whole was characterised by a lack of funds because its activities were never budgeted at project design, leaving the committees' survival after closing uncertain.
card.killed_note: No deaths are recorded in the completion report or the Independent Evaluation Group's review. The report notes that the project had no grievance procedure at contractor level, which could have helped document and monitor complaints by workers.
card.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,054 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The project's own subproject resettlement plans of March 2010 count planned impacts city by city: 279 households in Arusha, 41 people in Mbeya, and about 29 households at Kikuyu and 21 at Chidaya village in Dodoma, where 3 buildings and 20 farmlands were to be compensated at the landfill site. The completion report gives no count of affected or relocated people at all, so there is no Bank outcome figure to set against ICIJ's.
card.outcome: The credits closed on 26 November 2020 and the completion report rated the outcome Satisfactory, as did the Independent Evaluation Group's review. The report records that payments to contractors were also often delayed for the same shortage of counterpart funds, which delayed contract execution and brought periodic complaints to the Bank from contractors. It says the delayed availability of counterpart funds is a portfolio-wide issue affecting other Bank-financed urban projects as well. Whether the people whose compensation was more than nine months late were eventually paid in full is not stated.
card.confidence_note: This is the thinnest of the eight entries from this batch. The harm is a delay: the completion report says resettlement plan implementation was often delayed, sometimes to over nine months, when local authorities lacked funds to compensate affected people, and that this delayed construction and raised complaints. It attaches no count of people to that delay, does not say which cities the nine months applied to, does not say how many complaints were made, and does not say whether anyone went unpaid at closing. All the counts of people and structures given above are planning figures from subproject resettlement plans of March 2010, not outcomes, and the completion report publishes no outcome figure for resettlement at all. The report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review both rated the project Satisfactory and the report says the subprojects complied with the resettlement plans. The lender is reporting on its own project and no independent account of compensation under this project was found. The project has eight city resettlement plans and a later valuation volume; the counts above come from three of them, Mbeya, Arusha and Dodoma. The Independent Evaluation Group's review prints no date on its pages; the 22 October 2021 date is the Bank's catalogue field for the document and is unverified at document level.

card.whole: By the completion report's count the project paved or rebuilt 253.6 kilometres of non-rural road against 140 at appraisal and a target raised to 220, built or rehabilitated 42.02 kilometres of stand-alone drains against 15 and a revised 31, built or rehabilitated 277 waste collection points against 231 and a revised 255, built or improved seven sanitary landfills with 17 cells against five and a revised seven, built or improved 11 bus, daladala and lorry stands with room for 1,471 vehicles against six stands and 600 vehicles at appraisal and a revised ten and 1,100, and delivered 29 gender-sensitive features, among them paved walkways, raised humps near schools, footbridges and a playground, against a target of 17 set at restructuring. 1,890,687 people were counted as direct beneficiaries against 952,806 at appraisal and a revised 1,741,000, and 1,278,053 as having access to improved bus stations, terminals or lorry stands against 543,721 and a revised 1,266,200. Waste reaching landfills rose from 28 per cent of the waste generated to 86 per cent, against 58 per cent at appraisal and a target cut to 40 per cent because the first landfill began operating in the third quarter of 2016 rather than 2013. Own-source revenue in the eight local authorities rose 457 per cent over the 2010 base year against 45 per cent at appraisal and a revised 100 per cent, which the report attributes partly to the cities' rapid growth and to plot sales, a major revenue source, counting inside that revenue. Spending on operation and maintenance reached 28 per cent of municipal expenditure against 16 per cent at appraisal and a revised 20; fees and charges covered 84 per cent of solid waste operating costs against 12 per cent at appraisal and a revised 25, and 95 per cent of bus and lorry stand costs against 65 and a revised 80 - though the report's financial analysis says solid waste charges and fees do not cover operating costs, which it calls a risk to the sustainability of the facilities. Seven local authorities had up-to-date strategic urban development plans and general planning schemes, both targets met, and all project-related grievances were recorded as addressed. Four indicators were dropped: up-to-date property valuations and property tax collected, after responsibility for valuation, billing and collection moved to the Tanzania Revenue Authority from 1 July 2016, and roads in good or fair condition and people with access to an all-season road, as measures the project did not control. Institutional strengthening work on urban planning systems, geographic information systems and own-source revenue was dropped after delays in mobilisation and the pandemic and taken up by a follow-on project, and solid waste and geographic information equipment contracts were ended by mutual agreement with suppliers who could not produce in time. The report's economic analysis of a sample of works puts the rate of return at 40 per cent with a net present value of US$65 million - 48 per cent for urban roads, 32 per cent for the Arusha landfill, 33 per cent for the Duga drainage, 13 per cent for the Tanga bus station and 12 per cent for solid waste in Tanga - against 22 per cent at appraisal over 94 per cent of project cost in the Evaluation Group's table, and says actual investment costs at appraisal prices were 10 per cent below expectations and benefits three times costs. Both the report and the review rate efficiency Substantial and the outcome Satisfactory. The project ran on three credits totalling US$343 million, of which US$340.37 million was disbursed; the US$12.5 million expected from the Danish government at approval is recorded as nothing at completion, and total cost came to US$340.37 million against US$355.5 million at appraisal. All these figures are the lender's own; no check from outside the World Bank Group was found.
card.conditions: The project was environmental category B, partial assessment, and triggered three of the Bank's policies: environmental assessment, involuntary resettlement and physical cultural resources, the last of which matters because the plans count graves, a shrine and several graveyards among the assets affected. Environmental and social impact assessments, environmental and social management plans and resettlement action plans were prepared for the prioritised subprojects in each local government area, under an environmental and social management framework and a resettlement policy framework, using funds from an earlier Bank project to pay the consulting firms. The appraisal document records that draft assessments and plans for each city were disclosed at the Bank on 2 February 2010 and in Tanzania on 5 February 2010, and the final versions at both on 5 May 2010. Affected people were identified and compensation amounts set in line with Tanzanian law and the Bank's resettlement policy, and the plans were reviewed and monitored by the President's Office and the Bank. Paying the compensation was the local government authorities' own responsibility, as counterpart funding, and the completion report records that they repeatedly lacked the money. Grievance handling committees were set up in every subproject area, trained on a manual the President's Office wrote, and kept logbooks of complaints; the report says their activities were never budgeted at design, that there was no grievance procedure at contractor level for workers, and that their functioning after the project closed was uncertain (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 13 May 2021).

companies.role: The company that held the land for the proposed Kurasini substation and its wayleave corridor, and that TANESCO paid Tshs 1,638,111,700 for it. The amendment records that three families in two houses had first been consulted and earmarked for compensation at that site, and that it was then established that those people had sold their land to this company (Amendment of Resettlement Action Plan, January 2014).

companies.name: Rail Assets Holding Company (RAHCO)
companies.role: The state body that then held Tanzania's railway land. TANESCO was allowed to put its new 132 kV line inside 30 metres of the centre line of RAHCO's railway wayleave at Ukonga, and because the land belonged to RAHCO the affected people were paid for improvements on the land only and not for the land (Amendment of Resettlement Action Plan, January 2014).
companies.desc: A Tanzanian state-owned company incorporated by the Railways Act 2002, which names it Reli Assets Holding Company Limited (the project's resettlement-plan amendment and this key use 'Rail'), and whose whole issued share capital was held by the Treasury Registrar. Its objects were to acquire the rail transport functions of the Tanzania Railways Corporation together with transferred property, rights and liabilities, to secure or provide rail infrastructure, and to develop, promote and manage rail infrastructure assets on behalf of the government; it held the Railway Infrastructure Fund on irrevocable trust and could delegate its powers, which the Act says should take the form of concessions where practicable. Under the Act a railway strip 15 metres wide in urban areas and 30 metres in rural areas either side of the track centre line was reserved for future rail development, and building in it needed the company's written permission. The Act was repealed on 28 February 2018 by the Railways Act 2017, which establishes the Tanzania Railways Corporation.

card.community: The project rebuilt transmission and distribution lines and substations in Dar es Salaam, Moshi and Arusha, and the wayleaves it needed ran through built-up suburbs. The completion report says changing the wayleave in the densely populated suburbs of Dar es Salaam was costly and slowed the works, and that no additional resettlement plans were prepared for resettlements that had not been foreseen. A resettlement audit the Bank commissioned in September 2017, shortly before closing, put the number of project-affected people under the on-grid component at 11,070. The audit concluded that the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy had been followed, though implementation tended to conform more closely to Tanzanian law and practice than to the Bank's standards, and that poor recordkeeping of resettlement activities impeded effective monitoring of resettlement and its impact. TANESCO's own amendment to the resettlement plan, dated January 2014, gives the detail. At Ukonga, where the new 132 kV line was routed within 30 metres of the centre line of the railway wayleave from the Factory Zone II substation at Gongo la Mboto to the Factory Zone III substation at Kipawa, it names 43 affected people one by one and what each lost. The entries against the names read, in the amendment's own words: part of house, part of uncompleted house, part of the house, part of house affected, part of the house and septic tank affected, part of house and toilet affected, fence and house, and in one case '75% of house affected, Borehole, Trees'. Many of the entries are kiosks, one of them 'Kiosk (3)'. Others are trees, sugar cane, maize, tomatoes, sweet tomatoes, cassava, pawpaw, bananas, orange and guava, vegetables, boreholes, a tank, fences, hedges and part of a foundation. The amendment publishes no totals by type of loss. The amendment describes these people as having encroached into the railway wayleave, says the Managing Director approved valuing and compensating them for exhausted improvements made on the land only, because the land belonged to the railway company, in order to meet the Bank's requirement and allow the contractor to continue with works smoothly, and records that the compensation paid came to Tshs 300,639,109.92. It states that these people were compensated so as to allow the contractor to proceed with the construction, and that at a meeting on 18 September 2011 at Ukonga Magereza the affected people asked TANESCO to pay for their property excluding land and to give them enough time to vacate, and asked that the actual end of the 30-metre corridor be demarcated before the final counting of the properties to be compensated. TANESCO's own comment on that request reads: 'Experience shows that after compensation payment even if you give them a year PAPs are normally slow to vacate freely; a close follow up will be needed.' At Kurasini, three families in two houses were first consulted and earmarked for compensation for the substation and its wayleave; the amendment says it was later established that those people had sold their land to a company, MPS Oil (T) Limited, since renamed Kurasini Oil Storage Company Limited, and the Tshs 1,638,111,700 compensation was negotiated with and paid to that company. At Mbagala, three named individuals agreed in a meeting on 13 June 2012 to give up their plots if compensated, valuation was completed and signed by the Chief Government Valuer and a payment schedule was sent to the District Commissioner at Temeke, but the plots were then not used because another site was provided, and the amendment does not say whether those three were paid. At Mzinga Creek, a last-minute change to the design of the Kurasini to Ubungo line required a new corridor and affected 16 households, which the report describes in the future tense as households that will be affected and then counts in the same passage as 16 project-affected persons. The completion report says compensation had been made for 13 of the 16 and not for 3, and that TANESCO was working on the paperwork; it says TANESCO approved a top-up compensation payment after the project was completed. The report's own lessons include that land acquisition and compensation should be completed before a project's effective date, and that a project should start immediately after compensation to avoid encroachers.
card.killed_note: No deaths are recorded in the completion report, the Independent Evaluation Group's review or the resettlement plan amendment.
card.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 2,351 for the GEF grant P092154, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's own figures are different again: the September 2017 resettlement audit put project-affected people under the on-grid component at 11,070, the January 2014 resettlement plan amendment names 43 affected people at Ukonga, and the completion report counts 16 affected households at Mzinga Creek. No document found gives a count of people actually relocated.
card.outcome: The credits closed on 29 September 2017 with compensation outstanding for 3 of the 16 households at Mzinga Creek; the completion report says TANESCO approved a top-up payment after the project was completed and before the report was finished. The Independent Evaluation Group's review says the completion report could usefully have provided an update on whether the compensation pending for the three remaining households at closing, nearly a year before the review, had been paid, and gives no such update. The Bank also cancelled four distribution packages over shortcomings in the bidding process and, after an inquiry by its Integrity Vice Presidency, imposed a sanction of debarment on two private companies that had submitted false financial documents in bids for project contracts. The 13 km Ubungo to Kurasini section could not be built under the project because a road expansion by the national roads authority affected the wayleave, and TANESCO was financing it with its own funds after closing.
card.confidence_note: The 43 named affected people at Ukonga, the amounts paid, the Kurasini and Mbagala sequences and the Managing Director's decision to pay for improvements only all come from TANESCO's own amendment to the project's resettlement plan, published by the Bank in January 2014. The 11,070 affected people, the 16 households at Mzinga Creek and the 3 left unpaid come from the Bank's completion report, which reports the findings of a resettlement audit the Bank itself commissioned; the audit report is not in the Bank's document archive: its list of 67 documents for the project holds no resettlement audit, only financial audit reports, and two title searches for one returned none. The lender and the implementing agency are therefore reporting on their own project and no independent account of these wayleaves was found. The amendment gives no totals by type of loss, and none has been worked out from its list here. The amendment also contradicts itself on the line it covers, its introduction describing a line from Factory Zone III (Gongo la Mboto) to Factory Zone II (Kiwalani) and its Ukonga section a line from Factory Zone II (Gongo la Mboto) to Factory Zone III (Kipawa). No document found says what happened to the three families at Kurasini after their land was bought by the oil storage company, whether the three Mbagala landowners were paid, or whether the three Mzinga Creek households finally received the top-up. The resettlement audit concluded that the Bank's resettlement policy had been followed. The Independent Evaluation Group's review prints no date on its pages; the 18 October 2018 date is the Bank's catalogue field for the document and is unverified at document level.

card.whole: By the completion report's count the project built or rehabilitated 184.4 kilometres of distribution line against a target of 282 kilometres set at the 2015 restructuring, and 37.1 kilometres of transmission line against 57.1, the row's comment putting the transmission figure at about 37.4 kilometres: 13 kilometres of the Ubungo to Kurasini section could not be built because the national roads agency's Mandela Road expansion took the wayleave, and the 1.3 kilometres at Mzinga Creek was still being procured and installed at closing, with completion expected on 31 March 2018. The borrower's own section of the report says the 132 kV southern ring circuit planned for Dar es Salaam, running from the Factory Zone III substation through Factory Zone II, Mbagala and Kurasini to Ubungo, was removed from the project's scope for that reason, so the ring circuit could not be realised in the time available. End-user voltage reached 220 volts against a target of 218 from a baseline of 190; losses in the project area fell from 28 per cent to 16.44 against a target of 21; collection efficiency rose from 70 per cent to 94 against a target of 95; 25.45 MW of grid-connected small power generation was installed against 17 MW at appraisal and a revised 25 MW; 85,000 prepaid meters were installed against a target of 60,000; and 30,933 households were connected under the on-grid component against a revised target of 25,000. On the off-grid side the rural energy agency concluded 65 subproject transactions against a revised target of 10, standard power purchase agreements covered 58.3 MW of installed capacity against a revised 20 MW, rural household connections reached 71,966 against a target of 40,000, 144,622 households were connected under that component against a revised target of 110,000, which the report converts to 694,189 people at 4.8 people a household, and 206,149 direct beneficiaries were recorded against 20,000 at appraisal and a revised 114,000. Two rows fell short: customer satisfaction at the utility was 62 per cent against a target of 75, a gap the report calls 13 percentage points, and community connections - dispensaries, health centres, secondary schools, staff houses, police posts and public lighting - came to 996 against 800 at appraisal and a revised 1,200. Activities cancelled: the customer management system with its trouble and resource management modules, and the centralised call centre and high-value customer cell, both over budget overruns, with the first later taken into another Bank project; and in 2009 the procurement of four distribution packages, after the Bank objected to shortcomings in the bidding and its settlement with Siemens AG required the preferred bidder in three of the four packages to withdraw. The report puts the project's economic rate of return at 13 per cent with a net present value of TZS 24 billion (US$19 million) at a 10 per cent discount rate, covering 99 per cent of project cost, with the grid component at 17 per cent against 31 per cent at appraisal; one of the two mini-grids analysed returned minus 9 per cent, and photovoltaic installations in institutions returned minus 13 per cent with a net present value of minus US$2 million, against 21 per cent and US$300,000 at appraisal. No rate of return for the project as a whole was given at appraisal, and the report sets out why it includes no financial analysis. Both the report and the Evaluation Group's review rate efficiency Modest and the outcome Moderately Satisfactory on a split rating. Spending came to US$143.67 million against US$171.88 million at appraisal, with no borrower contribution, and the project closed five and a half years after its original date. All these figures are the lender's own; no check from outside the World Bank Group was found.
card.conditions: The project was environmental category B and triggered six safeguard policies: environmental assessment, natural habitats, physical cultural resources, involuntary resettlement, safety of dams, and projects on international waterways. An environmental and social impact assessment was prepared in 2005 for the on-grid transmission lines and an environmental audit was done at the substations to be upgraded; TANESCO updated the assessment and the documents were disclosed in 2007. A resettlement action plan for the transmission lines and substations in Dar es Salaam, Moshi and Arusha was disclosed in July 2007. A resettlement policy framework and an environmental and social management framework were prepared for the off-grid component and disclosed in 2007; the Rural Energy Agency found them hard for subproject developers to use and had them rewritten by a consultant in June 2012, translated into Kiswahili and redisclosed as a revised framework and a Resettlement Management Framework. TANESCO prepared and disclosed the amendment to the resettlement plan in January 2014 to cover additional resettlement caused by civil works in Dar es Salaam. The completion report states that no additional resettlement plans were prepared for the resettlements that had not been foreseen, and the Bank commissioned a resettlement audit in September 2017 instead, ahead of closing (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 27 June 2018).
